metadata.file_name: Reassessing urban-rural education disparities  evidence from England.pdf
metadata.title: Reassessing urban-rural education disparities: evidence from England

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 data for England, with a stratified two-stage sampling design described by the TIMSS program. The analytic sample is restricted to 8th-grade students with available school geography classification (urban vs rural vs missing) and includes cases with missing school questionnaire responses handled via an explicit “missing” category. The manuscript does not report applying TIMSS student/school sampling weights or any replicate-weight variance estimation, and it instead relies on OLS regression with adjusted R-square and coefficients plus descriptive effect sizes/odds ratios. Because the analysis is not framed as a complex-survey-weighted estimation procedure, readers should treat the reported associations as descriptive/correlational rather than fully design-representative estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 data for England. Schools were grouped into urban (densely populated urban areas, suburban areas, and medium-sized cities/large towns) versus rural (small towns, villages, remote rural areas). Because 43 schools did not respond to the school-level questionnaire, the analysis created a third “missing” group for students whose school geography was missing (883 cases). For real-valued variables with missingness, missing values were replaced by the mean in the regression models; for categorical variables (notably highest parental education), missingness was handled by adding an explicit “unknown” category.

main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS regression: Adjusted R-square step 1 = 0.191; step 2 adds School location (Rural) with coefficient = -0.083 and adjusted R-square = 0.198 (R-square change = 0.007).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics data for England, the study leveraged Home educational resources, Parental education level, Gender (sex), Math extra lessons, and School location (rural vs urban) to predict Math achievement (Plausible Values), finding that attending a rural school was negatively associated with math scores even after controlling for student background, explaining about 0.7% additional variance (adjusted R-square from 0.191 to 0.198; coefficient for rural = -0.083). This indicates that rural-school disadvantage in mathematics persists beyond SES and out-of-school learning, suggesting policy should target rural resource and support gaps rather than assuming geography effects disappear after accounting for family background.

main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS regression: Adjusted R-square step 1 = 0.202; step 2 adds School location (Rural) with coefficient = -0.050 and adjusted R-square = 0.206 (R-square change = 0.004).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science data for England, the study leveraged Home educational resources, Parental education level, Gender (sex), Science extra lessons, and School location (rural vs urban) to predict Science achievement (Plausible Values), finding that attending a rural school remained negatively associated with science scores after controlling for background variables, with only a small residual association (adjusted R-square from 0.202 to 0.206; coefficient for rural = -0.050). This indicates that rural disadvantage is present but weaker in science than in mathematics, implying that interventions may need subject-specific emphasis and should still address rural learning conditions and supports.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 data for England (N=3,365 students across 136 schools) to reassess urban–rural education disparities in mathematics and science. It creates an urban vs rural school geography grouping and a third “missing” group for students whose schools did not respond to the school questionnaire; missing real-valued variables are mean-imputed and missing parental education is handled via an “unknown” category. Achievement outcomes are TIMSS plausible values for math and science, and the regression models use OLS with stepwise forward entry of student background controls followed by a rural-school indicator. The rural-school indicator shows a negative association with achievement in both domains, with small explanatory power: adjusted R-square increases from 0.191 to 0.198 in math (rural coefficient = -0.083) and from 0.202 to 0.206 in science (rural coefficient = -0.050). The study is cross-sectional and does not report design-weighted estimation, so results should be interpreted as correlational rather than causal.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The manuscript reports regression-based prediction of achievement (OLS) and descriptive effect sizes/odds ratios, but it does not evaluate any machine-learning algorithms (e.g., Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM) and does not report ML model selection or ML performance metrics beyond adjusted R-square and coefficients. Therefore, the ML technique fields are left empty rather than inventing algorithms. The extracted findings still reflect a predictive modeling approach (regression) but not an ML algorithmic pipeline.
